uncited: Shadow Mapping for Volumes adapts the standard image-based shadow mapping technique to participate in light transport within volumetric data.
It solves the problem of determining whether a sample point along a view ray is occluded by the volume itself when viewed from a light source.
The method consists of two passes: a shadow map construction pass (preprocessing) and a rendering pass.
*   **Input:** Volumetric dataset, light source position and direction (for directional lights) or position (for point lights), transfer function (for alpha shadow maps).
**Standard Shadow Map:** A 2D texture storing depth values.
Each texel stores the distance from the light source to the first surface hit along the light ray.
**Alpha Shadow Map:** A 2D texture storing multiple layers.
Each layer consists of a pair: $(d_i, \alpha_i)$, representing depth and transparency.
*   Render the volume from the light source's perspective.
*   For each pixel in the light-space image, trace a ray through the volume.
*   Identify the first hit point (entry point) of the ray into the volume.
*   Evaluate an error function to determine if further sampling is needed.
*   Project $P$ into light space to obtain coordinates $(u, v)$.
*   Retrieve the depth value $d_{shadow}$ from the shadow map at $(u, v)$.
*   Compute the distance $d_{sample}$ from the light source to $P$.
*   **Binary Decision:** Compare $d_{sample}$ with $d_{shadow}$.
*   If $d_{sample} > d_{shadow}$, the point is in shadow.
*   If $d_{sample} \le d_{shadow}$, the point is lit.
*   Apply a **shadow threshold** to mark the intensity limit.
*   Standard shadow maps only support opaque occluders.
*   Precision issues may arise from depth buffer resolution limits, leading to shadow acne or peter-panning.
A variant of shadow mapping that supports semi-transparent occluders.
It differs from standard shadow mapping by incorporating multiple layers of depth and transparency for each pixel.
Instead of a single depth value, it saves control points of piecewise linear functions that approximate the volume's attenuation profile along the light ray.
This allows for more accurate shadowing in translucent volumes.
Choose this when visual fidelity of shadows in semi-transparent media is required, accepting higher memory and preprocessing costs.
*   **Time Complexity:** Preprocessing is $O(N_{light\_pixels} \times N_{samples})$, where $N_{light\_pixels}$ is the shadow map resolution and $N_{samples}$ is the number of samples per light ray.
Rendering is $O(N_{view\_pixels} \times N_{view\_samples})$ with a constant-time shadow lookup.
*   **Memory Complexity:** $O(W \times H)$ for the shadow map, where $W, H$ are the shadow map dimensions.
Alpha shadow maps require more memory per texel due to multiple layers.

The technique was developed by Timo Ropinski (University of Münster) and others (Markus Hadwiger, Patric Ljung, Christof Rezk Salama) as part of advanced illumination techniques for GPU-based volume raycasting.
